unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 2 pairs two information texts about astronomy and life on the space station with The Burrow Discovery, a story about a school science fair. Learners study twenty-five words such as burrow, boycott, glare, cooperate and ownership, and they master indefinite pronouns, singular agreement and adverbial phrases. They separate fact from opinion, compare biography with autobiography, and write a friendly blog post of their own.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and the twenty-five words. Read the two space texts, then the three parts of The Burrow Discovery. Answer the comprehension questions with quoted evidence. Work through the six grammar sections on indefinite pronouns, contractions and adverbs. Complete the six vocabulary and text activities. Record the speaking tasks, draft and revise the blog post, then finish with the quiz and self-assessment.

readings.title: The Night Sky Above Us
readings.setting: A highland town, its school and the wider world of space science
readings.passageScript:
For thousands of years, people have looked at the night sky and wondered what lies beyond.
Long before telescopes existed, careful observers in Africa, Asia and the Americas tracked the stars.
They built observatories on high ground, mapped the patterns they saw, and shaped brass instruments for measuring angles.
Their patient work became the source of much of the knowledge we still use in astronomy today.

One early astronomer spent thirty years checking the position and brightness of every star he could see.
He wrote his results in a book of fixed stars, listing hundreds of them in careful order.
His measurements were so accurate that everyone who studied the sky afterwards used the book as a guide.
Nobody had produced anything so complete before, and copies of it travelled from country to country.
Many star names in that book later crossed into English, which is why we still say Aldebaran and Betelgeuse.

Centuries later, the dream of exploring space became real.
In 1957, the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched into orbit around the Earth.
This was a booming moment in history, and it changed everything.
Scientists began to cooperate across borders, sharing ideas and instruments as they worked towards the Moon.
In 1969, astronauts landed on the Moon for the first time, and millions of people watched.

readings.title: Life on the Space Station
readings.setting: A highland town, its school and the wider world of space science
readings.passageScript:
Today the International Space Station orbits our planet about four hundred kilometres above the ground.
Astronauts from many countries live and work there for months at a time.
They conduct experiments, grow salad leaves, and study how the human body reacts to weightlessness.
The towering rockets that carry them into orbit are marvels of careful engineering.

Everything on the station must be planned in advance, because there is no shop in space.
If anything breaks, the crew must repair it themselves with the tools they already have.
Nobody can rush up with a spare part, so a small fault can become a serious issue.
That is why every astronaut trains for years before a single launch.

Space exploration is not only about science.
It teaches the value of cooperation, patience and steady hard work.
When people avoid conflict and aim at a shared goal, they can achieve brilliant results.
Whether you dream of becoming an astronomer, an engineer or a teacher, the stars are worth studying.
As the saying goes, the sky is not the limit; it is only the beginning.

readings.title: The Burrow Discovery, part 1
readings.setting: A highland town, its school and the wider world of space science
readings.passageScript:
The week of the school science fair had arrived, and everyone in Year 5 had a display to finish.
Amal stood beside her table with Nora and Sami, straightening a tray of damp soil.
"Our project is about animal homes," Amal explained to the visitors crowding round.
"We built a model burrow, and we can show how a rabbit lives inside it."
Sami adjusted the small grey object resting on top of the model.
"This is our soil sensor," he said proudly. "It tells us how moist the ground is."
"It tells us nothing at all," teased Nora. "Yesterday it refused to work."
Sami rolled his eyes. "We fixed it last night. You will see."
Later that morning, Teacher Yasmin made an announcement.
"Listen carefully, everyone. School science blogs are booming, and the town council has set up a competition.
You will write about your project, and the winners will present at the town library."
"Brilliant!" said Nora. "We are going to win."
Amal smiled. "Only if everyone does their part."
They began typing their blog post on the school tablets.
Amal wrote the opening: "Our group studied animal homes and built a model burrow.
It was hard work, but we cooperated well."
Nora added a warning of her own: "You'll want to avoid cheap glue. Our tunnel collapsed twice!"
Sami typed the strangest part last.
"While we were collecting materials, we found a glowing object in the field.
At first we misunderstood it completely. We thought it was plastic, but it was a piece of a meteorite."
Amal laughed. "Explain that clearly, or people will think we are describing a science film."

readings.title: The Burrow Discovery, part 2
readings.setting: A highland town, its school and the wider world of space science
readings.passageScript:
The class read every blog aloud before voting, and the room grew noisy with opinions.
Leo's group had built a windmill from card, wire and two small bulbs.
"Our towering windmill model produces light," Leo announced. "The glare from the bulbs proves it works."
"That glare is hurting my eyes," Maya whispered from the back row.
Sami sighed as he sat down. "Our project doesn't light up. Maybe we'll lose."
"You should relax," said Amal. "This is a school fair, not an empire falling."
Nora giggled. "Still, a win would be rather nice."
On the fair day, families crowded into the hall and the head teacher gave a short speech.
"Today we celebrate cooperation, careful observation and hard work," she said warmly.
"Unless somebody objects," whispered Nora.
"Nobody will," Sami whispered back, "unless we destroy the model before lunch."
The three of them laughed behind their hands.
Their model behaved perfectly. The burrow stayed standing, and the sensor beeped at exactly the right moment.
Afterwards a visitor came to their table with a notebook and a kind, curious smile.
"I am Elena, an engineer with the science youth council," she said. "Where did the source of this idea come from?"
"We watched rabbits digging near the road," Amal answered.
"We wanted to expose how animals build cool, dark places to rest in the hot season."
"The sensor was my part," Sami added. "A film about energy gave me the first clue."
"You seem very loyal to your work," Elena said. "That patience matters in science."

readings.title: The Burrow Discovery, part 3
readings.setting: A highland town, its school and the wider world of space science
readings.passageScript:
That afternoon Teacher Yasmin gathered the class to hear the blog results.
"The winning team is Amal, Nora and Sami," she announced, and the room erupted.
"You will present at the town library next week," she said when the cheering faded.
"You will also join a local energy project. Your task is to reduce the glare from public lights and consume less electricity."
"Another project?" asked Sami, suddenly feeling drowsy.
"You mustn't nap yet," laughed Nora. "This is a great chance."
The next morning they were walking to the community hall when they saw pupils holding painted signs.
Two of them were struggling to hoist a long banner above the doors.
"What is happening?" asked Amal.
"They are starting a boycott of plastic cups in the lunchroom," Maya explained.
"They want to protect the environment, and they say the waste is a real issue."
"Should we join them?" asked Nora.
"I would rather research it first," said Sami. "Nobody should sign anything they have not read."
So they talked to the group leader, who showed them his figures and a simple contract.
Hundreds of cups were used every week, and none of them were recycled.
"You have our approval," said Amal. "We will help you announce it next week."
"Taking ownership of a problem is the first step," Nora added, signing her name neatly.
The hall was not an ideal meeting place, but it was free and everybody fitted inside.
They wrote one last blog entry that evening, taking turns at the keyboard.
"Today we joined a group of pupils who want to end plastic cups in our lunchroom.
We cooperated, shared ideas and wrote a plan. Not everyone agrees yet, but we are working on it.
We also learned that nothing in science happens quickly, so you have to be patient.
Mix loyalty, effort and curiosity, though, and the results can be brilliant."

grammar.title: Indefinite pronouns: talking about people and things in general
grammar.explanation: Indefinite pronouns stand in for people or things when we do not need to name them exactly. One short word can replace a whole list, which keeps writing smooth and clear.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Instead of writing "Amal and Nora and Sami all cooperated during the experiment", we can write "Everyone cooperated during the experiment".
The word everyone replaces the three names and refers to all the people in the group.
Indefinite pronouns fall into three families.
People: everyone and everybody mean all people; someone and somebody mean an unknown person; anyone and anybody mean any person at all; no one and nobody mean not a single person.
Things: everything means all things; something means an unknown thing; anything means any thing at all; nothing means not a single thing.
Quantity: many means a large number; few means a small number; several means more than two; some means an unspecified amount; none means not any; all means the whole amount.
Examples: Everyone is welcome at the fair. Someone left a bag in the hall. Nothing was left behind. Several pupils volunteered. None of them were late.
These pronouns let us talk about unknown people, make general statements, ask open questions and write clear negatives.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers sometimes keep the list and the pronoun together, as in "Amal and Nora and Sami everyone cooperated". Choose the names or the pronoun, never both at once.
grammar.memoryTip: Indefinite means not fixed. If you cannot point at the exact person or thing, an indefinite pronoun is the word you need.
grammar.practice:
Part A: sort these pronouns into people, things and quantity: everybody, nothing, several, anybody, everything, few, no one, some.
Part B: rewrite each sentence so one indefinite pronoun replaces the underlined list. 1. Amal, Nora and Sami finished early. 2. The glue, the card and the wire were missing.
Part C: write three sentences about your school, one using a people pronoun, one using a things pronoun and one using a quantity pronoun.
Check yourself: Part A: people - everybody, anybody, no one; things - nothing, everything; quantity - several, few, some. Part B: 1. Everyone finished early. 2. Everything was missing. Part C is open-ended - model example: "Everyone helped tidy the classroom. Something surprised me at the fair. Several pupils stayed late to help."

grammar.title: Singular verbs after everyone, nobody and something
grammar.explanation: Most indefinite pronouns for people and things are singular, even when they describe a large group. They take singular verbs such as is, has, was, does and knows.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Correct: Everyone is ready for the presentation.
Correct: Nobody knows where the book went.
Correct: Something was glowing in the field.
Correct: Everything has been checked twice.
Wrong, then right: Everyone are happy becomes Everyone is happy.
Wrong, then right: Nobody know the answer becomes Nobody knows the answer.
Wrong, then right: Something were strange becomes Something was strange.
Wrong, then right: Everything have been packed becomes Everything has been packed.
Quantity pronouns behave differently: many, few and several count as plural, so we write Many enjoyed the show and Few had seen a rocket.
grammar.commonMistake: Everyone are excited and Nobody know the answer both sound right when spoken quickly. Slow down and say everyone is, nobody knows.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture everyone, someone and nobody as one person standing in for the whole group. One person always takes a singular verb.
grammar.practice:
Part A: correct the verb in each sentence. 1. Everyone are invited to the school fair. 2. Everything have been packed for the trip. 3. Somebody have eaten my lunch. 4. Nobody know the answer. 5. Everything have been cleaned in the lab.
Part B: choose is or are. 1. Nothing __________ more important than working together. 2. Many __________ waiting outside the hall.
Part C: write two sentences about the science fair, one starting with Everyone and one starting with Nothing.
Check yourself: Part A: 1. Everyone is invited to the school fair. 2. Everything has been packed for the trip. 3. Somebody has eaten my lunch. 4. Nobody knows the answer. 5. Everything has been cleaned in the lab. Part B: 1. is 2. are. Part C is open-ended - model example: "Everyone is proud of the science fair. Nothing was left unfinished by the end of the day."

grammar.title: Someone or anyone? Statements, questions and negatives
grammar.explanation: Use someone, somebody and something in positive statements. Use anyone, anybody and anything in questions and in negative sentences. No one, nobody and nothing already carry the negative inside them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Positive: Someone called you this morning.
Question: Did anyone call me?
Negative: I did not hear anything.
Positive: Something is wrong with the computer.
Question: Is anything wrong?
Because no one, nobody and nothing are already negative, adding not creates a double negative that reverses your meaning.
Correct: Nobody was late for class. Incorrect: Nobody was not late for class.
Correct: There is nothing in the box. Incorrect: There is not nothing in the box.
Correct: I cannot find anything in my bag. Incorrect: I cannot find nothing in my bag.
grammar.commonMistake: I can't find nothing in my bag uses two negatives, so it really claims that the bag is full. Write I can't find anything in my bag instead.
grammar.memoryTip: Some for statements, any for questions and negatives. No one and nothing already say no, so they never need not beside them.
grammar.practice:
Part A: choose the correct pronoun. 1. __________ wants to go outside for break. (Everyone / Anyone) 2. Does __________ know where the library book is? (someone / anyone) 3. __________ was missing from the science kit. (Something / Anything) 4. __________ in the class passed the test. (No one / Anyone) 5. We looked everywhere, but we could not find __________. (something / anything) 6. __________ of the students finished early. (Few / Nothing) 7. __________ is more important than working together. (Nothing / Anything) 8. Has __________ seen my notebook? (somebody / anybody)
Part B: fill each blank with someone, anyone or no one. 1. __________ should check the equipment before we start. 2. Is __________ coming to the meeting today? 3. __________ remembered to bring the map. 4. I do not think __________ noticed the mistake. 5. __________ volunteered to clean the classroom. 6. __________ in the group has ever visited a space centre.
Part C: repair the double negatives. 1. Nobody don't know the answer. 2. I can't find nothing in my bag.
Check yourself: Part A: 1. Everyone 2. anyone 3. Something 4. No one 5. anything 6. Few 7. Nothing 8. anybody. Part B: 1. Someone should check the equipment before we start. 2. Is anyone coming to the meeting today? 3. No one remembered to bring the map. 4. I do not think anyone noticed the mistake. 5. Someone volunteered to clean the classroom. 6. No one in the group has ever visited a space centre. Part C: 1. Nobody knows the answer. 2. I can't find anything in my bag.

grammar.title: Their after a singular pronoun, and contractions in a blog
grammar.explanation: Modern English uses their to refer back to a singular indefinite pronoun, which avoids the clumsy phrase his or her. Blog writing also uses contractions, because they make the voice sound friendly and spoken.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Everyone should bring their own lunch.
Somebody left their backpack in the classroom.
Nobody wanted to miss their chance to present.
Notice that the verb stays singular while the belonging word becomes their.
Contractions join two words and mark the missing letters with an apostrophe.
you will becomes you'll, we have becomes we've, they are becomes they're, it is becomes it's, must not becomes mustn't.
In the story the team revised their blog and used you'll, we've and they're so it sounded real.
Save contractions for informal writing such as blogs, letters to friends and dialogue.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers sometimes stretch a sentence into Everyone should bring his or her own lunch. Their is shorter, accepted and far easier to read.
grammar.memoryTip: One person for the verb, their for the belonging word: Somebody has left their coat.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite each sentence using their. 1. Everyone must bring his or her permission slip by Friday. 2. Nobody wanted to lose his or her place in the queue.
Part B: contract the underlined words. 1. You will present at the library. 2. We have finished the model. 3. They are starting a boycott. 4. You must not nap yet.
Part C: write two blog sentences about the science fair, each using one contraction and one indefinite pronoun.
Check yourself: Part A: 1. Everyone must bring their permission slip by Friday. 2. Nobody wanted to lose their place in the queue. Part B: 1. You'll present at the library. 2. We've finished the model. 3. They're starting a boycott. 4. You mustn't nap yet. Part C is open-ended - model example: "We've built our volcano model, and everyone is ready to present it."

grammar.title: Adverbs and adverbial phrases that answer when, where and how
grammar.explanation: Adverbs and adverbial phrases add detail by telling the reader when, where, how or how much something happens. One well-chosen phrase can turn a plain sentence into a picture.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Time: in 1969, every day, finally, last night.
Place: on the Moon, at the space centre, beside the launch pad.
Manner: carefully, patiently, with great effort, proudly.
Plain: The astronauts landed. Improved: In 1969, the astronauts landed on the Moon.
Plain: Scientists study the stars. Improved: Scientists study the stars patiently, every single day.
Plain: The crew checked the equipment. Improved: The crew checked the equipment carefully before the launch.
An adverbial phrase can open a sentence, sit in the middle, or close it, and the position changes the emphasis.
Commas usually follow an adverbial phrase that opens a sentence.
grammar.commonMistake: Piling three adverbs into one sentence buries the action. Choose the single phrase that answers when, where or how most usefully.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask when, where and how. Each answer you can give is an adverb or adverbial phrase waiting to join your sentence.
grammar.practice:
Part A: improve each sentence with one phrase from the box: in 1969, carefully, on the Moon, with great effort, finally, every day, at the space centre, patiently. 1. The astronauts landed. 2. Scientists study the stars. 3. The crew checked the equipment. 4. The rocket launched. 5. They trained for years.
Part B: write three sentences about the science fair, one with an adverb of time, one with an adverb of place and one with an adverb of manner.
Part C: move the adverbial phrase in one of your sentences to a new position and explain what changes.
Check yourself: Part A sample answers (other phrase choices from the box can also work if they still answer when, where or how): 1. In 1969, the astronauts landed on the Moon. 2. Scientists study the stars patiently, every day. 3. The crew checked the equipment carefully. 4. Finally, the rocket launched at the space centre. 5. They trained for years with great effort. Part B and Part C are open-ended - model example: "Last night, our class watched a meteor shower. We waited at the school field, and we spotted three shooting stars quickly. Moving the phrase "Last night" to the end changes the emphasis so the time feels like an afterthought rather than the main point."
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Editing a blog draft for agreement, negatives and punctuation
grammar.explanation: Good writers revise one feature at a time. Reading a paragraph aloud exposes verb agreement slips, double negatives and missing punctuation faster than reading it silently.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Pass one: check that every indefinite pronoun has the right verb.
Pass two: hunt for double negatives and replace nothing with anything where not is already present.
Pass three: check apostrophes in contractions and possessives.
Pass four: check that speech marks open and close around every spoken line.
Pass five: read the whole paragraph aloud and ask whether the meaning survived your changes.
Sample draft to repair: Everyone are excited about the fair. Nobody don't know the winner yet. Somebody have left they're notebook on the desk.
Repaired: Everyone is excited about the fair. Nobody knows the winner yet. Somebody has left their notebook on the desk.
grammar.commonMistake: Changing words without rereading the whole paragraph often breaks a meaning that was already correct. Reread the sentence before and after every change you make.
grammar.memoryTip: Read it, notice it, revise it, then read it once more.
grammar.practice:
Part A: edit this draft and mark five changes: Everyone are excited about the trip. Nobody don't know the time. Everything have been packed. Somebody have left they're bag. I can't find nothing in it.
Part B: swap drafts with a partner and check each other's contractions and speech marks.
Part C: explain in two sentences how two of your changes made the meaning clearer.
Check yourself: Part A corrected draft with five changes marked: "Everyone is[1] excited about the trip. Nobody knows[2] the time. Everything has[3] been packed. Somebody has[4] left their[4] bag. I can't find anything[5] in it." (1. are to is, 2. don't know to knows, 3. have to has, 4. have to has and they're to their, 5. nothing to anything). Part B is a partner-check activity with no single fixed answer - as a self-check, compare your five corrections above with a partner's or reread them aloud yourself. Part C is open-ended - model example: "Fixing 'Everyone is' instead of 'Everyone are' makes the subject and verb agree. Changing 'nothing' to 'anything' removes a double negative so the sentence means what it should."

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Astronaut interview role-play
speaking.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with a partner, or with your AI Tutor, with an adult nearby if one is available. One of you is a journalist and the other is an astronaut who has just come home from a mission.
The journalist asks at least five questions. Try these: What was the most brilliant discovery you made in space? Was there anything that surprised you about living on the station? How did the crew cooperate during difficult moments? Did everyone on the crew have the same job? What advice would you give to someone who dreams of flying?
The astronaut answers in full sentences, using at least four unit words and three indefinite pronouns.
Model line for the astronaut: "Nothing prepared me for the view, and everybody on the crew stopped work to look."
Model line for the journalist: "Was there anything about the towering rocket that frightened you on launch day?"
Swap roles and record the second interview so you can hear how your voice changes.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the journalist and interview me about a space mission, then tell me whether my answers used complete sentences and unit vocabulary.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Fact or opinion? Listen and decide
speaking.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Your teacher or an adult reads you a list of statements about space. If neither is available, your AI Tutor can read the statements aloud instead. After each one, say fact or opinion and give the clue that helped you.
Statements to start with: The Moon orbits the Earth. Space travel is the most exciting thing in the world. The space station has been in orbit since 1998. Everyone should learn about astronomy. Sputnik 1 was launched in 1957. Stars are the most beautiful things in the sky.
Model answer: "That is a fact, because the date can be checked in an encyclopaedia."
Model answer: "That is an opinion, because the word most beautiful tells us what the speaker feels."
Finish by discussing with your partner how you tell the two apart when a text mixes them together.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Read me six short statements about space, one at a time, and check whether I can label each as fact or opinion with a reason.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Group presentation of a science mission
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
In a small group, plan a pretend science mission and give it a name. Decide where you will go, what you will study, what equipment you need, and how the team will cooperate.
Every member presents one part of the plan, so agree who takes which section before you begin.
Use at least three unit words and two indefinite pronouns in your section of the talk.
Model opening: "Our mission is called Deep Burrow, and everybody in our team has one clear job."
Model closing: "Nothing will be wasted, because we will consume less power than the mission before ours."
Listen to another group and ask them one question that begins with How or Why.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my part of a group mission plan and tell me whether my section connects clearly to the sections before and after it.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Reading the winning blog aloud
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose one paragraph from the team's blog in The Burrow Discovery and prepare to read it aloud to the class.
Mark where you will pause, which words you will stress, and where the friendly blog voice should rise.
Read it once quietly, once to a partner, and once to the class or the recorder.
Model line: "We cooperated, shared ideas and wrote a plan, but not everyone agrees with us yet."
Ask your listener to name one thing that went well and one thing to improve next time.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to me read a blog paragraph aloud and comment on my pauses, my stressed words and my pace.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Should our school hold a boycott?
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Hold a four-minute discussion in a group of four about ending plastic cups in the lunchroom.
Take turns: one person speaks, the next builds on what was said, and nobody interrupts.
Use the sentence frames: "I agree with Nora because...", "I see it differently, because...", "Could you explain what you meant by...?"
Bring one fact and one opinion to the discussion and label them as you speak.
End by agreeing on one action your class could take this term, and say why it earned the group's approval.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Take the opposite view in a short discussion about plastic cups and check whether I answer your points instead of repeating my own.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Vocabulary expert interview
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose six unit words that you find hardest, and write one question about each.
A partner interviews you as the class vocabulary expert, and you answer in complete sentences.
Model exchange: "What is the difference between an object and a source?" "An object is a thing you can touch, while a source is where something comes from."
Give one real example for every word so the listener can picture it.
Swap places and interview your partner about six different words.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me as a vocabulary expert about six Unit 2 words and tell me which definitions were still too vague.

writing.title: Writing 1: A space discovery blog post
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine that you are a young astronaut writing a blog post about your first week on the International Space Station. Write in an informal, friendly tone, as if you were chatting with your family back home.
Include at least five unit words and underline them.
Include at least four indefinite pronouns and write them in bold.
Use contractions such as I'm, we've, it's and you'll so the voice sounds spoken.
Describe one surprising thing you discovered, and add a short paragraph on how the crew cooperates.
Finish with a closing sentence that encourages your readers to keep exploring.
Write between 150 and 250 words.
writing.modelText: Hello from orbit! You'll never guess what happened on my third day. Everyone was busy with experiments when something drifted past the window, and nobody could name it at first.
writing.sentenceStarter: You won't believe what happened during my first week...
writing.expectedLength: 150 to 250 words in four short paragraphs
writing.successCriteria: I used an informal blog voice; I underlined five unit words; I marked four indefinite pronouns; I used contractions; I described one surprise; I closed with encouragement
writing.support: Use the planning questions: what was most exciting, what did you see from the window, how does the crew work together, what would you tell your family?
writing.extension: Add one fact you checked and one opinion of your own, then label them for your reader.

writing.title: Writing 2: The same astronaut, two ways
writing.promptAndInstructions:
A biography is the story of a life written by somebody else, in the third person, focusing on facts and achievements.
An autobiography is written by the person themselves, in the first person, and includes feelings and memories.
Write two short paragraphs about the same astronaut. Paragraph one is biography, paragraph two is autobiography.
Keep the same three facts in both paragraphs so the reader can see how the viewpoint changes.
Underline every pronoun you use, and check that the third person and first person never mix.
writing.modelText: Biography: She became the first woman to command the space station, and her calm decisions impressed the whole crew. Autobiography: I remember gripping the handrail on my first morning in command, wondering whether anyone could hear my heart.
writing.sentenceStarter: She trained for six years before...
writing.expectedLength: Two paragraphs of about sixty words each
writing.successCriteria: I kept the same three facts in both paragraphs; I used third-person pronouns in the biography; I used first-person pronouns in the autobiography; I added feeling to the autobiography only
writing.support: List your three facts first, then write each one twice, once with she and once with I.
writing.extension: Add one sentence of reported speech to the biography and one of direct speech to the autobiography.

writing.title: Writing 3: Information page about the space station
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write an information page for a younger class about the International Space Station.
Begin with a clear heading, then write five accurate facts as separate numbered points.
Use precise unit vocabulary, and keep every sentence to one fact.
End with one sentence that tells the reader where they could find out more.
Check spelling, capital letters and full stops before you hand it in.
writing.modelText: Living and Working in Orbit. 1. The station circles the Earth about four hundred kilometres above the ground. 2. Crews stay on board for months and consume carefully packed meals.
writing.expectedLength: One heading and five numbered facts
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; I gave five separate facts; every fact can be checked; I used three unit words; I named a place to find out more
writing.support: Reread Life on the Space Station and highlight five sentences that state facts rather than opinions.
writing.extension: Add a short glossary of three unit words with your own definitions.

writing.title: Writing 4: An opinion paragraph about plastic cups
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Should your school stop using plastic cups in the lunchroom? Write one paragraph that states and defends your viewpoint.
Open with a topic sentence that makes your opinion clear.
Give two reasons, each supported by a fact or a figure from the story.
Answer one objection that somebody might raise against you.
Close with the action you want your reader to take.
writing.modelText: Our school should end plastic cups this term. Hundreds of cups are used every week, and none of them are recycled, so the waste is a real issue.
writing.expectedLength: One paragraph of eight to ten sentences
writing.successCriteria: I opened with my opinion; I gave two supported reasons; I answered one objection; I kept the same viewpoint throughout; I closed with a clear request
writing.support: Use the connectives because, however and therefore to join your reasons together.
writing.extension: Rewrite your closing sentence twice, once politely and once forcefully, and say which suits your reader.

writing.title: Writing 5: Fair day from Sami's viewpoint
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Retell the science fair day from Sami's viewpoint, in the first person.
Begin at the moment the sensor beeped and finish when Elena walks away from the table.
Show how Sami feels about the sensor he built, using his own thoughts rather than a narrator's.
Use at least three unit words and two contractions.
Keep every event that happens in the story, but change nothing about the order.
writing.modelText: The sensor beeped at exactly the right second, and I finally let my shoulders drop. Nobody knew how many nights I'd spent repairing it.
writing.sentenceStarter: The sensor beeped, and I finally...
writing.expectedLength: Three paragraphs of about seventy words
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the first person throughout; I kept the story order; I showed Sami's feelings; I used three unit words; I used two contractions
writing.support: Underline every sentence in part 2 that mentions Sami before you begin planning.
writing.extension: Add one short paragraph telling the reader what Sami plans to build next.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and improve
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose one earlier piece of writing from this unit and improve it.
Revise three sentences so the meaning is clearer, and add two useful details.
Correct every double negative and every verb that disagrees with its indefinite pronoun.
Write two sentences explaining what you changed and why the change helps your reader.
Read the finished piece aloud one last time before you submit it.
writing.modelText: I changed Everyone were excited to Everyone was excited, because everyone is singular. I also added on the launch pad so the reader knows where the rocket stood.
writing.sentenceStarter: The change that helped my reader most was...
writing.expectedLength: One revised piece plus two sentences of explanation
writing.successCriteria: I revised three sentences; I added two details; I fixed the agreement errors; I removed every double negative; I explained two of my changes
writing.support: Use the five editing passes from the grammar section, one pass at a time.
writing.extension: Ask a partner to read the old and new versions and tell you which is clearer, and why.

Read the two passages and decide which is from a biography and which is from an autobiography. Give the pronouns that prove it.
Passage A: "I was so nervous before my first spacewalk. My hands were shaking inside my gloves, but I told myself to stay calm. When I opened the hatch, everything below me looked peaceful."
Passage B: "She graduated from university in 2005 and joined the space programme three years later. Her team described her as one of the most dedicated astronauts they had ever worked with."
Then list two more differences between the two text types, thinking about who wrote them and what each one focuses on.
activities.answerSummary: Learners sort two passages by viewpoint, quote the pronouns as evidence and list two further differences.

activities.title: Activity 6: Prefix detective
activities.instructionsAndItems:
A prefix is a group of letters added to the front of a word to change its meaning.
Prefix clues: astro means star; tele means far; auto means self; tri means three; mis means wrongly; re means again.
Work out and write the meaning of each word using the prefix and the root.
1. astrodome. 2. teletext. 3. autobiography. 4. triennial. 5. resupply. 6. misread.
Then find two more words in this unit that begin with one of the six prefixes above.
activities.answerSummary: Learners use six prefixes to work out the meaning of six words, then hunt for two more prefix words in the unit.

assignments.title: Exploring Space learning portfolio
assignments.instructions:
Submit two pieces: the blog post from Writing 1, and a recording of the astronaut interview from Speaking 1.
Revise both pieces first, using the Grade 5 writing and speaking rubrics printed in this unit.
Marking guidance for the teacher. Award the writing marks from the four writing criteria: ideas, organisation, language and conventions, four marks each.
A level four blog keeps a friendly informal voice throughout, underlines five unit words used accurately, marks four indefinite pronouns with matching verbs, and closes by encouraging the reader.
A level two blog uses the vocabulary but slips into essay register, or marks fewer than four pronouns.
Award the speaking marks from the four speaking criteria: clarity, vocabulary, sentence accuracy and interaction, four marks each.
A level four interview answers in complete sentences, uses at least three indefinite pronouns correctly, and extends each answer with a reason or an example.
Deduct nothing for accent or hesitation; assess only clarity, accuracy and the ideas expressed.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the correct verb after an indefinite pronoun?
quizzes.options: Everyone is ready for the presentation. | Everyone are ready for the presentation. | Nobody know the answer yet. | Everything have been packed.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Everyone is ready for the presentation.
quizzes.explanation: Everyone is singular, so it takes the singular verb is. The other three sentences pair a singular pronoun with a plural verb.

quizzes.question: What does the word burrow mean?
quizzes.options: A large area of land ruled by one government | A very bright light that is hard to see in | A hole or tunnel that an animal makes in the ground to live in | A written agreement between two or more groups
quizzes.correctAnswer: A hole or tunnel that an animal makes in the ground to live in
quizzes.explanation: A burrow is an animal home dug into the ground. The other options define empire, glare and contract.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses anyone correctly?
quizzes.options: Anyone left a bag in the hall. | Did anyone see my notebook? | Anyone has been using the tablets today. | Anyone is more important than teamwork.
quizzes.explanation: Anyone belongs in questions and negatives. The other three are statements, which need someone, somebody or nothing.

quizzes.question: Which sentence avoids a double negative?
quizzes.options: Nobody was not late for class. | There is not nothing in the box. | I can't find nothing in my bag. | Nobody was late for class.
quizzes.explanation: Nobody already carries the negative, so no extra not is needed. The other three sentences say the opposite of what the writer meant.

quizzes.question: According to The Night Sky Above Us, in which year was the first artificial satellite launched?
quizzes.explanation: The passage dates the launch of Sputnik 1 to 1957. The Moon landing came in 1969, twelve years later.

quizzes.question: Which unit word describes somebody who feels sleepy and wants to rest?
quizzes.explanation: Drowsy means sleepy. Loyal describes faithfulness, towering describes height and booming describes loudness.

quizzes.question: Which of these statements about space is an opinion rather than a fact?
quizzes.options: The Moon orbits the Earth. | Sputnik 1 was launched in 1957. | The space station has been in orbit since 1998. | Stars are the most beautiful things in the sky.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Stars are the most beautiful things in the sky.
quizzes.explanation: Most beautiful signals a personal view that cannot be checked. The other three statements can be verified in a reference book.

quizzes.question: In The Burrow Discovery, what did Sami build for the team's model?
quizzes.options: A painted banner | A soil sensor | A card windmill | A glass telescope
quizzes.explanation: Sami built the soil sensor that measures moisture. The windmill belonged to Leo's group and the banner to the boycott pupils.

quizzes.question: The prefix mis in the word misunderstood tells you the action was done in which way?
quizzes.explanation: The prefix mis means wrongly, so misunderstood means understood wrongly. The prefix re means again.
quizzes.origin: Curriculum-reviewed item authored from the Grade 5 Unit 2 sources

quizzes.question: What are people doing when they take part in a boycott?
quizzes.options: Refusing to buy or use something to show they disagree | Lifting a heavy load to the top of a pole | Signing a written agreement about shared rules | Telling everybody a piece of important news

teacherNotes.note: Model each new word aloud and check meaning before independent work. Mix written, spoken and drawn responses so every learner can show understanding. Give feedback on complete sentences, quoted evidence and vocabulary precision rather than neatness. An adult must stay present whenever learners use the AI Tutor or a recording device, and no child should be left alone with the device.

The source pack offers four tutor moments, and each is safe only with an adult in the room. First, meaning checks such as asking what cooperate means or for an example of an indefinite pronoun. Second, comprehension hints such as asking the tutor to help find one fact and one opinion in the space passage. Third, grammar coaching on when to use someone rather than anyone. Fourth, writing support such as asking for an opening line for a blog about living in space. Ask learners to bring the tutor's answer back to the class for checking, so the tutor supports thinking instead of replacing it.
